newsitem.title: CANADA: Floods, U.S. CRP may cut Canada wheat acres - WEFA.
newsitem.headline: Floods, U.S. CRP may cut Canada wheat acres - WEFA.

text.p: Western Canada wheat acreage forecasts were likely to be revised downward due to spring flooding, more wheat acreage expected on the U.S. northern Plains and export delays in Canada, a grain analyst said.

Hugues Rinfret, Canada agriculture analyst for Pennsylvania-based consultants WEFA Inc, forecast Western Canada wheat harvested acreage in the coming year at 29.4 million acres, versus 30.72 million last year.
"You might go down to 28.7 (million) from the 29.4 (million) we're forecasting now," Rinfret told reporters after addressing a Canada Grains Council meeting here.
He cited more harsh weather in Manitoba this week.
"This snowstorm in Manitoba's going to affect acreage," Rinfret said. "It'll delay planting."

Manitoba's Red River Valley had double the snow and moisture accumulation by April 7 compared to last year, while the U.S. side of the valley had three times the average accumulation, water management and weather officials said.
Both regions are usually heavily planted to spring wheat.
Rinfret told the council meeting that Canadian seeding intentions would also be influenced by how many acres from the U.S. Conservation Reserve Program end up planted to wheat.
About 21 million to 22 million CRP acres expire this year, he said.

Montana had the most eligible acreage to expire this year, followed by North and South Dakota, all key spring wheat states that may add to supply and lower prices, Rinfret said. The U.S. Freedom to Farm law also adds planting flexibility.
"Wheat and canola in Canada has experienced a lot of acreage volatility in the last four to five years, and the U.S. is about to experience this as well," he added.

The U.S. Agriculture Department said April 1 that farmers had offered to enroll 18 million expiring 1997 acres along with 7.5 million new acres in CRP, with spring wheat states North Dakota and Montana ranking second and third in offers.
USDA has until mid-June to take up the offers, based upon budget and quality of the acreage offered.

In its first estimate of spring wheat plantings on March 31, USDA said farmers expected to plant 20.9 million acres this year against 23.6 million last year. Winter wheat acreage is 48.2 million acres, down from 51.9 million last year.

Rinfret said a third factor which may limit Canadian wheat seeding was likely higher than expected Canadian end-season wheat stocks on August 1 due to a winter export backlog that saw one ship wait as long as 62 days to load last month at Canada's Pacific coast.
"Some say (wheat) exports won't reach 17.5 million tonnes and it all depends how much we can catch up from this winter's delays," Rinfret said.
The added stocks would add to domestic supplies and could lower Canadian Wheat Board Pool Return projections, discouraging more wheat plantings.
